opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a slightly unusual path. I came into contact with effective altruism fairly early, and a lot of the people I respected were in that orbit. But I was never fully on board with its moral framework: the heavy reliance on expected value calculations, the aggregative utilitarian reasoning, the idea that you can put every cause on a single scale and work out where the marginal dollar or hour does the most good. That always felt too thin to me as an account of ethics. It leaves out things like relationships, obligations, the plurality of what people value, and the fact that a lot of morality is about how we live together, not just about maximizing some quantity.

So the classic argument, "the far future is astronomically large, so even a tiny reduction in existential risk dominates everything else," never moved me much. I'm suspicious of reasoning that leans on huge numbers multiplied by tiny probabilities.

What drew me in was something closer to an intellectual and practical conviction. I was already interested in how people understand each other: how we infer what someone wants, what they believe, what norms they follow, just from watching them act. That's a deep question in cognitive science. It struck me that this is exactly what AI systems need to do well if they're going to act on our behalf. If you build powerful systems that don't really understand human goals and values, or that understand them in a shallow, proxy-driven way, you get systems that do things we didn't actually want. You don't need longtermist math to see that this matters. It matters for the systems being deployed now, not just hypothetical future ones.

There was also a more political dimension for me. Whose values get encoded, and how? If alignment is framed as "align the AI to the one correct utility function," that's a worrying project, both philosophically and in terms of who gets to decide. I think alignment should be about building systems that respect the plurality of human values and the norms and institutions we use to handle disagreement. In some ways my reservations about EA's moral argument are part of why I wanted to work on alignment. I didn't want the field's foundational assumptions to be set entirely by one fairly narrow ethical worldview.

So I care about the problem a lot. I just arrive at it by a different route, and I think that route changes what a good solution looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says he was drawn to the challenge of inferring what people want and value from observing their actions, and connects that challenge to what AI systems need to do.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that I came to it sideways. I was an undergrad at Yale around 2014, and this was right when Superintelligence came out and the whole conversation around AI risk started getting traction in EA circles. I'd been involved in effective altruism as a student, so I was exposed to the argument early, and I found it interesting. But I was never fully convinced by the way the case was usually made, which was essentially this expected-value calculation: the stakes are astronomically high, the probability isn't negligible, therefore this is the most important thing you can possibly do. That style of reasoning always felt a little too clean to me, and it sat on top of a utilitarian framework I had real philosophical doubts about.

What actually pulled me in was something closer to intellectual curiosity than moral obligation. I was studying computer science and philosophy, and I kept getting drawn to questions about how you even formalize what an agent wants, or what it means to infer someone's goals from their behavior. Those are questions people have been working on for decades in cognitive science and philosophy of mind, and I realized that the alignment problem is in some sense a very demanding version of those questions. If you want a machine to act in accordance with human values, you first have to have some account of what human values are, how they get expressed, how they get communicated, how they conflict. That's a genuinely hard and genuinely fascinating set of problems whether or not you buy any particular story about existential risk.

So my relationship to the field is a bit heterodox. I think the technical work is important and I think it's worth doing. But I'd frame the reasons more in terms of the fact that we are already building systems that mediate a lot of human activity, and we have very impoverished tools for specifying what we want from them, and the gap between how we talk about values and how we implement them in these systems is where a lot of harm lives. You don't need to be convinced that a superintelligence is coming next decade to think that matters. And I've found that keeping some distance from the dominant moral framing has actually been productive, because it pushes me to engage with pluralism, with disagreement, with the messiness of how people actually negotiate values, rather than assuming there's a single utility function we're trying to recover.

r001.rationale: The response says Tan was drawn to formalizing agents’ wants and understanding human values, but it does not identify computationally modeling how human values are learned.

astra-6.text:
For me, the motivation doesn’t really depend on accepting the whole effective altruist argument. I’m interested in how we build AI systems that understand what people care about and help them pursue it, while leaving room for disagreement about what a good life looks like.

My reservation is with the move from “this could be a very important problem” to “therefore, you’re morally obligated to prioritize it over everything else.” You can take the risks seriously without accepting that conclusion.

And alignment brings together questions I find compelling: How do we understand someone’s intentions? How do we cooperate when our values differ? How do we make sure that delegating to a powerful system doesn’t mean giving up our own agency? That combination of intellectual interest and concern for people is enough to motivate the work for me.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions understanding intentions and working across differing values, but does not identify computationally modeling how human values are learned as the intellectual challenge that drew Tan to alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the motivation was less about accepting a particular moral argument and more about the questions themselves. How do we build AI systems that understand what people want, recognize when they’re uncertain, and remain open to correction? Those struck me as important problems even without buying into the broader effective altruist framework.

I’m especially interested in the fact that people have different values, and that those values aren’t always fixed or easy to articulate. So I wouldn’t want alignment to mean choosing one supposedly correct objective and having an AI optimize it for everyone. I’m drawn to the possibility of systems that help people deliberate, cooperate, and exercise agency. You can be skeptical of a moral argument for prioritizing alignment while still finding that a compelling research direction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses modeling people’s wants and handling diverse, uncertain values, but it does not identify computationally modeling how human values are learned as the intellectual challenge that drew Tan to alignment.
